chunks: As for what al-Saffar narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Abdullah ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn Mahziyar, who said:

Bundar, the master of Idris, wrote: 'O my master, I vowed to fast every Saturday.' He wrote back and I read it: 'Do not leave it except due to an excuse, and you are not required to fast it during travel or illness unless you intended that. If you broke your fast in it without an excuse, then give charity for the count of each day to seven poor people. We ask Allah for success in what He loves and is pleased with.'

So it does not contradict the first two reports, because the way to reconcile between them is that the expiation is only obligatory according to the capacity of the person. Whoever is able to free a slave, that is required of him; if he is unable, he feeds seven poor people; if he is unable to do that as well, there is nothing upon him. And thus we said regarding one who intentionally breaks a fast in the month of Ramadan, and upon this we have collected the reports.
ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for failing to fulfill a vow to fast on specific days?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this correspondence from Ali ibn Mahziyar, highlighting the juristic principle that kaffarah is graded according to the individual's financial capacity (taqah), ranging from freeing a slave to feeding the poor. This flexible approach ensures that vows remain attainable and is explicitly extended by the scholar to the expiation for intentionally breaking a Ramadan fast, demonstrating a harmonization of hadiths through proportional liability.
